"What happened? As it relates to Affirm specifically: o Black Friday spending trends were supportive of current guidance o Delinquency rates are holding steady (also supported by ABS data) o AFRM’s avg FICO score is around 650 (higher if calculated on volumes) – with only 12% of their book comprised of developing credit and subprime consumers o International volume growth will likely become more material in 2027 and beyond – so no change to our expectation there • What does this mean for the stock? We attribute the underperformance to increasing concerns about the broader health of the lower-income consumer, though we expect AFRM to deliver steady credit quality trends in a relatively stable environment. The company continues to demonstrate how it is benefitting from multiple secular growth tailwinds (geography, verticals, and new users) as well as its best-in-class execution around risk management and credit deployment." title: The hiring rate in America is dropping significant...
content:
The hiring rate in America is dropping significantly, signaling a major shift in how businesses view the economic future. 
In October, the total nonfarm hiring rate fell to 3.2%, the slowest pace since the pandemic bottom in 2020. 
Even more concerning, over the past four years this rate has declined 1.4 percentage points to levels matching December 2008, right in the depths of the financial crisis. 
The private sector tells an even grimmer story, with hiring dropping to 3.5% in October, the lowest since January 2011. 
To understand how severe this is, consider that during the 2001 recession the hiring rate stayed higher at 3.7%-4.0%. 
We're now at or below crisis level lows without even being officially in a recession.
When hiring rates collapse this quickly, it reveals that businesses have lost confidence in near term growth and are shifting from expansion mode to preservation mode.
 This matters because what happens in hiring doesn't stay isolated, it creates a cascading effect throughout the economy. 
Slower hiring means fewer people entering the job market and less wage growth pressure, which reduces consumer spending power. 
When consumers spend less, companies see lower revenues, which forces them to hire even less, creating a downward spiral. 
For individuals, this means the tight job market is rapidly loosening, making it harder to find employment and negotiate raises. 
For the broader economy, weakening hiring signals weaker consumer spending ahead, which puts pressure on corporate earnings and forces the Federal Reserve to consider more aggressive interest rate cuts. 
Essentially, the labor market that's been one of the economy's strongest supports is showing serious cracks, and that weakness will reverberate through inflation expectations and consumer confidence.
The US labor market is coming to a halt:
The total nonfarm hiring rate fell -0.2 percentage points in October, to 3.2%, the lowest since the 2020 pandemic bottom.
Over the last 4 years, this figure has declined -1.4 percentage points, to levels in-line with December 2008.
By comparison, during the 2001 recession, the hiring rate was much higher, at 3.7%-4.0%.
Furthermore, the private hiring rate fell to 3.5% in October, the lowest since January 2011 and in-line with the 2020 lows.
The US labor market has stalled. 
- 
The Kobeissi Letter

title: More than 9 million US borrowers miss student loan...
content:
More than 9 million US borrowers miss student loan payments as delinquencies rise. 
For the last 12 months, the government enforced a safety net called the on-ramp which stopped student loan servicers from reporting missed payments to credit bureaus. 
It effectively blinded the system to the fact that millions of people were not paying their debts. 
The sudden spike in the numbers isn't because a massive wave of people stopped paying yesterday, it is because the credit bureaus are finally processing a year long backlog of shadow delinquencies all at once. 
We are seeing the official data catch up to reality, revealing that millions of Americans have been technically in default for months but the system was just forbidden from acknowledging it until now.
This exposes a widespread gamble that didn't pay off. 
A huge number of these borrowers likely stopped paying strategically, either betting that the government would eventually forgive the loans or simply choosing to spend their money elsewhere because there was no penalty for skipping the student loan bill. 
That period of consequence free non payment is over. 
The economic fallout from this is going to be painful. 
As these missed payments finally hit credit reports, millions of people are watching their credit scores crash, which immediately freezes them out of the market for mortgages and car loans. 
You can't qualify for a home loan when your credit report shows serious delinquency so this pulls a massive layer of demand out of the housing market. 
Even worse, as these borrowers are forced to scramble and start paying again to fix their credit, they have to pull cash away from restaurants, travel, and retail. 
It sucks spending power out of the fun parts of the economy and redirects it into paying off old interest, acting as a brake on growth just when the economy needs consumers to keep spending.

title: Fed Chair Powell says. "We can raise and lower int...
content:
Fed Chair Powell says. "We can raise and lower interest rates, but we don't really have the tools to address a secular housing shortage, structural housing shortage."
On December 10, the Fed cut interest rates to a range of 3.5%–3.75% to help the economy but Powell explicitly warned that this financial move won't fix the "structural housing shortage" facing the country. 
He is admitting that the Fed’s tools are mismatched for the actual problem at hand.​
Here is what he means by "structural" or "secular" shortage, the US housing market is broken at a fundamental level, not just a temporary one. 
Since the 2008 financial crash, homebuilders have built far fewer homes than necessary to keep up with population growth. 
We are now missing millions of homes due to strict local zoning laws, high construction costs, and a lack of skilled labor. 
Because these are physical and legal barriers, no amount of tweaking interest rates can magically cause new neighborhoods to appear.​
The implication for you and the economy is a bit of a trap. 
Many people are waiting for interest rates to drop so they can finally afford a home but Powell is warning that lower rates might actually make home prices jump higher.
If the Fed makes borrowing cheap (stimulating demand) while the number of houses remains flat (restricted supply), you get more buyers fighting for the same few homes. 
This leads to bidding wars that erase the savings you would have gotten from the lower mortgage rate.​
Ultimately, Powell is shifting the responsibility. 
He is telling the public and politicians that the Fed has done what it can do.
 Fixing the housing crisis isn't about monetary policy anymore; it requires Congress and local governments to change laws so that builders can actually build. 
Until supply increases, housing will likely remain a problem regardless of what the Fed does with rates.
"Housing is going to be a problem," Fed Chair Powell said. "We can raise and lower interest rates, but we don't really have the tools to address a secular housing shortage, structural housing shortage. https://t.co/neMU2W4N7s
